analysis.one_liner: Treats US companies that move headquarters abroad as domestic for tax purposes.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 7, 2024 with 10 cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and received no markup, vote, or floor action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a US company redomiciles overseas to cut its US tax bill but its owners and management stay in America, this bill would keep taxing it as a domestic company. It lowers the shareholder-ownership threshold that triggers that treatment from 60 percent to 80 percent, adds a test based on where a company's management actually sits, and applies the rules back to the end of 2014. The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who otherwise absorb a larger share of federal costs when large corporations lower their US tax bills by redomiciling abroad, plus US-based companies that keep their headquarters in the United States and would compete on a more even footing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and companies that stay US-based

how_it_helps.text: The bill treats a foreign corporation as domestic for US tax purposes if former shareholders of the US company own 80 percent or more of it, down from the current 60 percent threshold, covering deals structured just below the line.

It adds a second trigger: a company whose management and control occur primarily in the United States and which has significant domestic business activity — at least 25 percent of employees, employee compensation, assets, or income in the US — is also treated as domestic, regardless of where its legal home is.
The rules apply to taxable years ending after May 8, 2014, reaching the wave of inversion deals completed over the past decade, not just future ones.

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations that have moved or want to move their legal headquarters abroad to lower US taxes, and their shareholders, who would face higher US tax bills under the bill's retroactive rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinationals that redomicle abroad to cut taxes

drawbacks.text: The rules are retroactive to taxable years ending after May 8, 2014, meaning completed mergers from up to a decade earlier could face new tax treatment with no advance notice — a disruption even supporters of closing inversion loopholes would have to weigh.

The bill exempts companies with substantial business activities in their new foreign country of organization, so firms that move genuine operations overseas along with their legal home would still escape US treatment, and some companies might respond by relocating management fully abroad rather than staying in the US.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific tax-avoidance structure — companies that keep their owners, managers, and much of their business in the US while claiming a foreign address for tax purposes — and its carve-out for companies with real foreign operations limits overreach. The sharpest objection is retroactivity: applying new rules to deals completed since 2014 upends settled transactions and creates uncertainty. On balance it is a narrow fix rather than a broad tax overhaul, and its practical effect hinged on regulations the Treasury would have had to write.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on May 7, 2024, and the record shows no markup, vote, or floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so it died in committee.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Durbin introduced the Stop Corporate Inversions Act of 2024 with eight Democratic cosponsors and Sen. Bernie Sanders on May 7, 2024.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
That referral is the only action recorded; the bill received no committee vote and never reached the Senate floor before the 118th Congress ended.

The bill would amend section 7874 of the tax code, which governs inverted corporations, by raising the ownership threshold from 60 to 80 percent and adding a management-and-control test, with retroactive effect to taxable years ending after May 8, 2014.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations that have already inverted or hold the option to invert keep the existing rules, which treat companies with 60 percent or more US ownership as domestic but leave room below that line, and companies with post-2014 inversion deals avoid retroactive tax changes.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Corporate Inversions Act of 2024 on May 7, 2024.

for.name: Democratic senators Dick Durbin's cosponsors (Reed, Whitehouse, Blumenthal, Hirono, Duckworth, Van Hollen, Baldwin)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republicans joined.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 7, 2024 and took no recorded action on it — no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independent (Sanders); no Republican signed on, and the bill drew no recorded floor activity in either direction.

industries.industry: Multinational corporations that have inverted or plan to (notably pharmaceutical and medtech firms)
industries.note: The bill would treat these companies as domestic for tax purposes retroactive to 2014, raising their US tax bills and ending the benefit of a foreign legal address. Their savings come at the cost of the US treasury and other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Companies with substantial genuine foreign operations
industries.note: The bill exempts companies with substantial business activities in their new foreign country, but the new management-and-control test could still pull in firms with significant US operations, so exposure depends on regulations Treasury would write.

industries.industry: US-headquartered companies that keep their domicile
industries.note: By closing the inversion route, the bill removes a tax disadvantage relative to rivals that redomicile abroad, leveling competition among companies serving US customers.
